We know that any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ has the form

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the coordinates relative to the basis $\,B.$ Since we are told that $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -4\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={{(\,8\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{{(\,-4\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}32 \\ -24 \\ -16\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-36 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -20 \\ -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\},$ where 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

If $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]$ then what is the value of ${x}_{1}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember, the order of the vectors in a basis is important.

Notice that 

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={{(\,1\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{{(\,0\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}}+{{(\,-3\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{3}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{3}}
$$

which means that

$$
x=1\cdot {b}_{1}+0\cdot {b}_{2}+(-3)\cdot {b}_{3}
$$

and therefore

$$
[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}],
$$

Finally, ${x}_{1}=1.$

questions.problem:
Find the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -10 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 8 \\ -20\end{aligned}].
$$

If $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ then what is the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2} & =x \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -10 \\ 6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 8 \\ -20\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above gives the system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 10 \\ 4 & -10 & 8 \\ -2 & 6 & -20\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 10 \\ 4 & -10 & 8 \\ -2 & 6 & -20\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 10 \\ 0 & 2 & -32 \\ -2 & 6 & -20\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 10 \\ 0 & 2 & -32 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=10 \\ 2{x}_{2}=-32.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-16.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-3(-16)=10\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-38.
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-38 \\ -16\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=(-38)+(-16)=-54.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{2} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

 Finally,  by substituting ${x}_{2}=1$  into the first equation we obtain

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding a Vector Given Its Coordinates Relative To a Given Basis
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the vector $\mathbf{x}$ if $\,\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \}$ is a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \},$ and
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/798c2f477907d0d3414eeed0a2f37871c69466d9b4a098699a364f6a034c0679.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We know that any vector in  $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \}$ has the form

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

where $x_1$ and $x_2$ are the coordinates relative to the basis $\,\mathcal{B}.$ Since we are told that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/de91d9b4cd4eabed0a27696d7bf0512c19f6c66eb3c81ab6dc6a73fc0a1c15a5.svg) we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={{(-1)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{{(\,3\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Coordinates of a Vector Relative To a Given Basis Containing Two Vectors
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \},$ where
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/c36abdf2587e3b457ef47d67b3df21d7b8de505202e4bc1f4629e3284c49b87b.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We need to find $x_1$ and $x_2$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2} & =x \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -11 \\ -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above gives the system with the augmented matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/e5b57b4f1488c927d64d89cb4352715b471025a111a39fe786c869973401fbd4.svg)

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -5 \\ 3 & 5 & -11 \\ 4 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -5 \\ 0 & -4 & 4 \\ 4 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -5 \\ 0 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & -12 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -5 \\ 0 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The augmented matrix above corresponds to the following system of equations: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=-5 \\ -4{x}_{2}=4\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x_2 =-1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
x_1 + 3 \left( -1 \right)  = -5
\qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
x_1 = -2.
$$

Therefore, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/286b19d6c3b5b3fac7f65ffd4adab1b175d4dab5fab1e5bb7a85da692f09224a.svg)

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Coordinates of a Vector Relative To a Given Basis Containing More Than Two Vectors
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \mathbf{b}_3 \},$ where
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/5d9d3780a503745f072cdb2e9cea0eedddca811143b05a2cc426480e93c8dac9.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We need to find $x_1,$ $x_2,$ and $x_3$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =x \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -9 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7 \\ 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above system as an augmented matrix $M$ and reducing using Gaussian elimination, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -9 & -1 & 7 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -9 & -1 & 7 \\ 0 & -3 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -9 & -1 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{4}{3} & \frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=1 \\ -9{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=7 \\ \frac{4}{3}{x}_{3}=\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $x_3 =2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
-9x_2 - 2 = 7 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x_2 = -1,
$$

and substituting $x_2=-1$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x_1+3(-1) = 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad x_1 = 4.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector Relative To a Given Basis Containing More Than Two Vectors

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Given a subspace $H$ with a basis $\mathcal B = \{ \mathbf b_1, \mathbf b_2 \}$ and a vector $\mathbf x \in H,$ the **coordinates of the vector** $\mathbf{x}$ **relative to the basis** $\mathcal{B}$ are the coefficients ${\color{red} x_1}$ and ${\color{blue} x_2}$ such that

$$
{\color{red}x_1} \mathbf{b}_1+{\color{blue}x_2} \mathbf{b}_2 = \mathbf{x}.
$$

We can write the vector $\mathbf x$ relative to the basis $\mathcal B$ using these coordinates, as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/0593ca6a838b66c4623e8749eb5236d6259b1f9bf36ed0d68b83c49781076341.svg)

To demonstrate, consider the basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \},$ where 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/f355faa0c477775f2a1cbb3522d0743cdbc9649a5ee9c55b579b1fac9ae2a661.svg)

Also let $H = \textrm{span} \{ \mathbf b_1, \mathbf b_2 \},$ and consider the vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/78357fcf51c9cd6b7873f5bc35fcc214cb3790bcec00ee69d0932f15aacd39cb.svg)

The vector $\mathbf x$ can be expressed as a unique linear combination of $\mathbf b_1$ and $\mathbf b_2.$ That is to say, there exist *unique coefficients* $\color{red}x_1$ and $\color{blue}x_2$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2} & =x \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Let's solve for these coefficients. From the above, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=8 \\ 2{x}_{2}=4\end{aligned}
$$

The unique solution of this system is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/82d4f494936d23e9b697aa4518edf68f7ea62e504d9d2576a6d13971acaf1c96.svg)

Therefore, we have that 

$$
\mathbf{x} = {\color{red}3} \mathbf{b}_1+ {\color{blue}2} \mathbf{b}_2,
$$

which can be visualized as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/94b2934727a32284e9790e59ccd301bd858a0258843314a2968285a5eda7a302.png)

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
Given a subspace $H$ with a basis $\mathcal B = \{ \mathbf b_1, \mathbf b_2 \}$ and a vector $\mathbf x \in H,$ the **coordinates of the vector** $\mathbf{x}$ **relative to the basis** $\mathcal{B}$ are the coefficients ${\color{red} x_1}$ and ${\color{blue} x_2}$ such that

$$
{\color{red}x_1} \mathbf{b}_1+{\color{blue}x_2} \mathbf{b}_2 = \mathbf{x}.
$$

We can write the vector $\mathbf x$ relative to the basis $\mathcal B$ using these coordinates, as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/0593ca6a838b66c4623e8749eb5236d6259b1f9bf36ed0d68b83c49781076341.svg)

To demonstrate, consider the basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \},$ where 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/f355faa0c477775f2a1cbb3522d0743cdbc9649a5ee9c55b579b1fac9ae2a661.svg)

Also let $H = \textrm{span} \{ \mathbf b_1, \mathbf b_2 \},$ and consider the vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/78357fcf51c9cd6b7873f5bc35fcc214cb3790bcec00ee69d0932f15aacd39cb.svg)

The vector $\mathbf x$ can be expressed as a unique linear combination of $\mathbf b_1$ and $\mathbf b_2.$ That is to say, there exist *unique coefficients* $\color{red}x_1$ and $\color{blue}x_2$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2} & =x \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Let's solve for these coefficients. From the above, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=8 \\ 2{x}_{2}=4\end{aligned}
$$

The unique solution of this system is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/82d4f494936d23e9b697aa4518edf68f7ea62e504d9d2576a6d13971acaf1c96.svg)

Therefore, we have that 

$$
\mathbf{x} = {\color{red}3} \mathbf{b}_1+ {\color{blue}2} \mathbf{b}_2,
$$

which can be visualized as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/94b2934727a32284e9790e59ccd301bd858a0258843314a2968285a5eda7a302.png)

tutorials.name: The Standard Basis
tutorials.problem:
Let's consider a set of vectors
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/0d78e1b2d01003885882f19b3856278e5024719f26f33594fd071fbd73273b71.svg)

Notice that the set $\mathcal{S}$ is linearly independent since the vector equation $x_1\mathbf{e}_1+x_2\mathbf{e}_2+x_3\mathbf{e}_3=\mathbf{0}$ leads to the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}
$$

which has only the zero solution. 

Also, notice that any vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{e}_1,$ $\mathbf{e}_2,$ and $\mathbf{e}_3.$ For instance,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/ef28dd8cbad6d256b9fa82c487263af3327ce630839cfcd1c7433417d0e0ae73.svg)

In particular, the equation above tells us that 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/724f42afb534edbde7588c5508a4bf8de6d3cd068bc2989da7c7207b1bf7a1ba.svg)
that is to say, the numbers $\color{red}-2,$ $\color{red}0,$ $\color{red}5$ are the coordinates of $\mathbf{v}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{S}.$ 

The basis $\mathcal{S}$ is somewhat special, since the coordinates of a vector relative to this basis coincide with the components of the vector. We refer to $\mathcal{S}$ as the **standard basis**. Remember that in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$ we even have special notations for the vectors of the standard basis:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/aee5dd3226ebe950defc8b873399a884e0679ce701a3a55354ef01960e029f8e.svg)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/dd96e0b70173adf8983feb4975c351ab3e417c34ed4a6a944bc391e33db4c8e9.png)

In general, the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/a8e4b648898c0dc036e228fb84945833dc40c053beff034596e098c4dd077e23.svg)

tutorials.title: The Standard Basis
tutorials.content:
Let's consider a set of vectors
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/0d78e1b2d01003885882f19b3856278e5024719f26f33594fd071fbd73273b71.svg)

Notice that the set $\mathcal{S}$ is linearly independent since the vector equation $x_1\mathbf{e}_1+x_2\mathbf{e}_2+x_3\mathbf{e}_3=\mathbf{0}$ leads to the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}
$$

which has only the zero solution. 

Also, notice that any vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{e}_1,$ $\mathbf{e}_2,$ and $\mathbf{e}_3.$ For instance,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/ef28dd8cbad6d256b9fa82c487263af3327ce630839cfcd1c7433417d0e0ae73.svg)

In particular, the equation above tells us that 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/724f42afb534edbde7588c5508a4bf8de6d3cd068bc2989da7c7207b1bf7a1ba.svg)
that is to say, the numbers $\color{red}-2,$ $\color{red}0,$ $\color{red}5$ are the coordinates of $\mathbf{v}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{S}.$ 

The basis $\mathcal{S}$ is somewhat special, since the coordinates of a vector relative to this basis coincide with the components of the vector. We refer to $\mathcal{S}$ as the **standard basis**. Remember that in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$ we even have special notations for the vectors of the standard basis:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/aee5dd3226ebe950defc8b873399a884e0679ce701a3a55354ef01960e029f8e.svg)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/dd96e0b70173adf8983feb4975c351ab3e417c34ed4a6a944bc391e33db4c8e9.png)

In general, the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274696/assets/a8e4b648898c0dc036e228fb84945833dc40c053beff034596e098c4dd077e23.svg)
